resources.string: Choose a folder: the app looks for the games of every console in it, up to four levels of folders down.
With All files access, games are read where they are: nothing is copied.
The app then asks how to read it: in place with All files access, or through Android\'s folder picker.

Games/

Reading the folder. Disc images are opened to find their title, so a large folder takes a moment.

Nothing in this folder looks like a game the app knows: an extracted Xbox disc (default.xbe), a disc image, or a GBA, PS1, N64 or GameCube file. Pick another folder, or continue and add one later from the library.
Game Boy Advance, PS1, N64 and GameCube games start at once, in the interpreter.
Xbox and Xbox 360 games are prepared first: translated for this device, once, plugged in. You start it from each game.
Change any of these later in Settings › General. Continue when you are done.

When a game\'s Home says it met code the preparation missed, preparing it again takes a few minutes and makes it run smoother. Answers to the usual questions are in Settings › General › Help and questions.
Why games are prepared, why preparing again is sometimes worth it, Self-healing, your saves.

A game is written for its console\'s processor. Prepare reads its code, rewrites it as code for this device\'s processor and compiles it, here on the device. The game then runs as native code, at full speed. It is done once per game; the app\'s fixes for the game and its optional enhancements come with it.
From a few minutes for a small game to much longer for a large Xbox game. The game\'s Home shows the time left. Keep the device plugged in; the preparation goes on if you leave the app.

Reading a game finds most of its code, not all of it: some is only reached while playing. When a game meets code the preparation missed, it goes on, slower there, and the app notes it; the game\'s Home then says so. Preparing again translates that code too, and it is quick: only what changed is compiled again. Prepare again is also offered after an app update that translates games better, for another version of the disc, or when you turn Enhancements on or off.

On by default. When a run met code the preparation missed, the app prepares the game again by itself: after a crash, then starts it again; after a good run, in the background while you keep playing. A note says so each time, and you can stop it. A crash with nothing new to learn is not retried: the game\'s Home says it needs a fix.
No. A preparation never touches your saves, and neither does an app update: they are kept apart from the prepared code. The library\'s Options › Storage exports them.
Why do some games start without preparing?

Game Boy Advance, PS1, N64 and GameCube games have an interpreter: they start at once. Preparing them makes them run natively, smoother and lighter on the battery. Xbox and Xbox 360 games have no interpreter here: they play once prepared.
This game is translated for this device before it plays: once, with the device plugged in. Afterwards it runs as native code.
Keep the device plugged in. You can leave the app: the preparation goes on, and Home shows the time left. Your saves are never touched.
Your last run met code the preparation had missed: it ran slower there. Preparing again adds it in a few minutes, as only what changed is compiled again. Play stays available meanwhile.
This version translates games better. The game plays as before; preparing it again gets the fixes. Your saves are kept.
This game runs in the interpreter, so it starts at once. Prepare translates it into native code (a few minutes): smoother, lighter on the battery. You can play meanwhile.
Your game speaks its console\'s language.
Here, x86 code, as in an Xbox game. This device understands arm64.
Every function is written again for this processor, then compiled on the device.
Some targets only show while playing.
« call [eax] »: the address exists only once the game runs. A run will find it.
You play. The game finds the address.
That part runs slower, in the interpreter, and the app notes it.
Only what changed is compiled again: a few minutes instead of a whole preparation.
For the curious: what does a translation look like?
A 20-second animation on a small function of our own: its x86 code written again in arm64 line by line, a call whose target only a run knows, and Prepare again adding it.
What happened to this game: each preparation, the code its runs found that the preparation missed, a crash that needs a fix.
Prepared before the app kept a journal: the journal starts here.
Code the preparation had missed: it ran slower there. The next preparation adds it.
The game crashed on code the preparation had missed. The next preparation adds it.
Nothing yet. Each preparation, and each run that finds code the preparation missed, adds a line here.

Your own dumps kept elsewhere (a NAS, a PC, a server) can show in the library before they are on the device: add a torrent of them, one per console (a private torrent is best). A on a game downloads it, then it is set up like any game. Downloads wait for Wi-Fi unless you allow mobile data. Library › Options › Network sources lists them later.
Games on the network are downloaded first: A on one in the library.
Can I play games I keep on another device?

Yes, with the network library. Make a torrent of your own dumps (one per console; a private torrent is best) and add it in Library › Options › Network sources, as a .torrent file or a magnet link. Its games show in the library with a cloud and « On the network ». A on one downloads only that game, then it is set up like any game: an Xbox game is prepared, the others play at once. Downloads wait for Wi-Fi unless you allow mobile data. The app ships no torrent and no catalog.
